report:
Archive notifications now survive a crash: each account a note was shared with gets exactly one notification for every archiving that was stored, however many times the server restarts. `yarn verify` passes (117 tests), and the work is committed as `24cd8bc` on the current branch, not pushed.

**How it works**
- **Recording an archiving:** the archive change and the list of notifications it owes are saved together in one SQLite transaction, in a new `archive_notices_owed` table. Cancelling the note's reminder is part of that transaction too. Either all of it is kept or none of it is, so an archiving that wasn't stored owes nothing.
- **Sending the notifications:** creating them and clearing what's owed happen together in a second transaction. A crash in between can't lose a notification or send it twice.
- **On startup:** `createApplication()` sends whatever is still owed before it serves any requests. Each notification keeps the time of the archiving, so the list stays in the right order.
- **The drill:** with `FAULT_DRILL=after-archive`, the server kills itself (SIGKILL) right after the first archiving is stored, before sending anything.
- **Store changes:** the store (`src/store.ts`) gained transactions. If one fails, its changes are undone in the database and in memory. SQLite now waits for each write to reach the disk (`synchronous = FULL`), so a power cut can't lose a write that has already finished.
- **The API** is unchanged, apart from one more table in the database file.

**Tests**
- **Real crash (`src/crash.spec.ts`):** a test starts the real server as a separate process with the drill on and archives a note. It checks that the process died from SIGKILL and that the database holds the owed notifications but none sent yet. It then restarts three times and checks that each recipient has exactly one notification every time.
- **Other cases in the same file:** a crash simulated in-process between storing and sending, the drill firing only on the first archiving, nothing owed after a normal archive, and a failed archiving giving no notification and leaving the note unarchived after a restart.
- **`src/store.spec.ts`:** saving, rolling back and refusing nested transactions, for both the in-memory and SQLite stores.

**What was unclear, and what I decided**
- **Which archivings the drill counts:** "The first archiving it records" could mean the first since the process started or the first ever. I took it as the first since this start; the process dies right after it anyway.
- **What the client sees:** the archive request runs before the server replies, so a crash leaves the client with no response and no way to check the outcome later. The archiving is still stored and its notifications still go out. The spec says the API doesn't change, so I left it like that.
- **Out of date `CLAUDE.md`:** it still says "Data is kept in memory; there is no database". That hasn't been true since the previous feature (`DATABASE_PATH`). I didn't edit it.

Changes that arrive at the same moment are no longer lost, including when several server processes share one database file. In the tests, 20 shares sent at once to 3 separate processes all succeeded and all were kept. `yarn verify` passes (133 tests), and the work is committed as `85d316f`, not pushed. The API is unchanged.

**How it works**
- **Several processes, one file:** each process used to keep its own in-memory copy of the data, loaded at startup. Now every read goes to the database file (or to memory without `DATABASE_PATH`), so a process sees at once what another recorded.
- **Every change runs in one transaction:** each command reads and writes inside a single transaction that holds the database for its whole run. Changes from different requests or processes take turns rather than overwriting each other. That's why an edit and a share sent together are both kept.
- **Refusals:** a command waits up to 5 seconds for another process to finish. If it still can't get in, it is refused with `ERROR` / `CONFLICT` and changes nothing. Each change takes a few milliseconds, so in practice commands wait their turn rather than being refused.
- **Knock-on fixes:**
  - **Sign-up:** the duplicate-email check and saving the new account now happen in the same transaction, so two processes can't create the same email twice.
  - **Archive notifications:** each owed notification is checked again just before it is sent, so two processes never send it twice. Sending happens only after the archive is saved; if the database is busy, it tries again shortly rather than reporting a kept archive as a failure.
  - **The crash drill** from feature 15 still fires right after the archive is saved.
  - **Ordering numbers** for notes and notifications are now assigned when each one is written, so different processes don't hand out the same number.
- **Tokens** stay per process, as the spec allows: a person signs in to each one.

**Tests**
- **One process, in memory and on file:** 20 shares sent at once all kept; an edit and a share sent at once both kept.
- **Three real server processes on one file:** a change made on one is visible on the others straight away; 20 shares sent at once across them are all kept on every process; an edit and a share sent to different processes are both kept; the same email signed up on all three at once gives exactly one account.
- **Store and refusals (`src/store.spec.ts`, `src/tracker.unit.spec.ts`):** a second connection holding the database gets a refusal, nested transactions roll back together, and a failed or refused command changes nothing.

**What was unclear, and what I decided**
- **When to refuse:** the spec allows refusing a change "because the note changed under it" but prefers fewer refusals. I made commands wait their turn and refuse only after a 5-second wait. I didn't add version checks on notes, because an edit and a share sent together must both be kept.
- **A remaining gap:** a command's outcome is saved in its own write after the change. If the database stayed held for more than 5 seconds at exactly that point, the change would be kept but its outcome request would fail with an error. That only happens under very heavy load.
- **Slower with large data:** reads now scan the whole table every time, so this gets slower as data grows. That's fine at this size; indexes would be the next step.
- **Blocking wait:** while a process waits for the database it is blocked and can't answer other requests.

When `NOTIFY_URL` is set, every notification a person receives is now also sent to the outside service, and resent until the service accepts it. `yarn verify` passes (140 tests), and the work is committed as `2f2d24b` on the current branch, not pushed.

**How it works** (new file `src/courier.ts`)
- **Nothing lost to a crash:** each notification is put in a new `outbox` table in the same database transaction that creates it. A notification that exists is always queued for sending, even if the server dies right after.
- **Sending:** about every 200 ms the server sends whatever is due: `POST {NOTIFY_URL}` with `{ id, recipientId, kind, noteId }`. The `id` is the same one `GET /notifications` lists.
- **Accepted:** only a `2xx` within 2 seconds counts. The notification then leaves the outbox and is never sent again.
- **Refused, failed or no answer:** it is sent again with the same body, after 0.5 s, then 1 s, 2 s, and every 4 s after that. So the first retry comes within a second and later ones at most about 4.2 s apart.
- **After a crash:** whatever is still in the outbox is sent once the server starts again. If it dies after the service accepted but before that was recorded, the same notification goes once more under the same id, which the service recognises.
- **Reminders** are sent when they come due, not when they are set. A reminder that is replaced or cancelled before then is never sent.
- **Several processes on one database:** a notification being sent is marked as taken for 3 seconds, so other processes don't send it at the same time.
- **Without `NOTIFY_URL`:** nothing is queued and nothing is sent.

**Tests (`src/outside.spec.ts`, against a fake service)**
- Each recipient of an archived shared note gets exactly one send, with the right id, recipient, kind and note id.
- Four refusals then an acceptance give five identical sends: the first retry within a second, none more than 5 s apart, and nothing after acceptance.
- A request left unanswered is sent again 2 to 3.5 s later.
- A reminder is sent only once due, and a replaced one is never sent.
- A real server process is killed with SIGKILL while the service is refusing; after a restart the same notification is delivered once, and a further restart sends nothing.
- Nothing is sent without a URL, and `NOTIFY_URL` is read from the environment.

**What was unclear, and what I decided**
- **When a reminder counts as received:** I took it to be the moment it comes due, the same moment `GET /notifications` starts listing it.
- **Notifications from before the URL was set:** notifications created while the server ran without `NOTIFY_URL` are not sent if it is later restarted with it.
- **Timing basis:** retries and due times use the application's clock, the one tests can move forward.
- **Stopping the server:** a send in progress when the server stops normally is abandoned and sent again on the next start. Its 3-second hold must run out first, so after a quick restart that retry can take up to about 3 seconds.
